gpc_catalase.mechanism: Detects the enzyme catalase, which converts H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂. This separates Staphylococcus and Micrococcus (catalase-positive) from Streptococcus and Enterococcus (catalase-negative). The distinction reflects fundamentally different strategies for handling reactive oxygen species.
gpc_catalase.procedure: Add a drop of 3% H₂O₂ to a colony on a clean slide or in a tube. Vigorous, immediate bubbling = positive. Never use colonies from blood agar — red blood cells contain catalase and will cause false positives.
gpc_catalase.tip: Distinction tip: If asked why you chose this test first, say: "Catalase status is the primary branch point in Gram-positive cocci identification because it divides the clinically significant organisms into two entirely different identification pathways." If plate findings are available, combine catalase with haemolysis pattern to prioritise likely organisms faster.

gpc_coagulase.mechanism: Free coagulase converts fibrinogen to fibrin, clotting plasma. This virulence factor is unique to S. aureus among clinically significant staphylococci. The tube test detects free coagulase; the slide test detects bound coagulase (clumping factor) — always confirm a positive slide test with a tube test.
gpc_coagulase.procedure: Inoculate 0.5 mL rabbit plasma. Incubate 37°C for 4h. Tilt tube — solid gel that does not flow = positive. If negative at 4h, re-read at 24h. Observe carefully: even a partial clot counts as positive.
gpc_coagulase.tip: Distinction tip: S. lugdunensis (a CoNS) possesses clumping factor and gives a false-positive on the slide test, but is negative on the tube test. Mention this in your answer to show you understand the limitation of rapid tests.

gpc_novobiocin.mechanism: Novobiocin inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II). S. saprophyticus has an intrinsic structural modification to its GyrB subunit that confers resistance. This distinguishes it from S. epidermidis, which is susceptible.
gpc_novobiocin.procedure: Place a 5 µg novobiocin disk on a blood agar plate inoculated with the organism. Incubate 37°C 24h. Zone of inhibition ≥16mm = susceptible (S. epidermidis); zone <16mm or no zone = resistant (S. saprophyticus).
gpc_novobiocin.tip: Distinction tip: S. saprophyticus resistant to novobiocin is the second most common cause of UTIs in young, sexually active women (after E. coli). The resistance is intrinsic, not acquired — it reflects the species's inherent biology, not antibiotic pressure.

gpc_pyr.mechanism: Detects the enzyme pyrrolidonyl peptidase, which cleaves the chromogenic PYR substrate, releasing a compound that reacts with cinnamaldehyde to produce a cherry-red colour. Only Enterococcus and S. pyogenes (Group A) are PYR-positive among catalase-negative cocci.
gpc_pyr.procedure: Touch colony to PYR-impregnated disk or substrate. After 2 min contact, add one drop of cinnamaldehyde reagent. Cherry-red colour within 1 min = positive. Orange colour is a weak positive; yellow = negative.
gpc_pyr.tip: Distinction tip: Only two catalase-negative cocci are PYR-positive: Enterococcus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Everything else is negative. This makes PYR one of the most discriminating single tests in Gram-positive identification.

gpc_nacl.mechanism: Tests osmotolerance. Enterococcus spp. can grow in high-salt environments because of their robust cell membrane and ion transport systems — an adaptation to their natural niche in the mammalian GI tract. S. pyogenes cannot tolerate this osmotic stress.
gpc_nacl.procedure: Inoculate brain heart infusion broth containing 6.5% NaCl. Incubate 35°C 24–48h. Visible turbidity = positive (growth = Enterococcus). No turbidity = negative (S. pyogenes).
gpc_nacl.tip: Distinction tip: Enterococcal osmotolerance, bile tolerance, and intrinsic antibiotic resistance all reflect adaptations to the GI tract. This robustness is exactly why VRE (vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus) is so difficult to eradicate from hospital environments.

gpc_optochin.mechanism: Optochin (ethylhydrocupreine HCl) disrupts ATP synthesis in S. pneumoniae by interfering with its membrane-associated ATPase. Other alpha-haemolytic streptococci have structurally different ATPases and are therefore resistant.
gpc_optochin.procedure: Place a 5 µg optochin disk on blood agar inoculated with organism. Incubate 35–37°C in 5% CO₂ for 24h. Zone of inhibition ≥14mm = susceptible (S. pneumoniae); zone <14mm or no zone = resistant.
gpc_optochin.tip: Distinction tip: S. pneumoniae is BOTH optochin-susceptible AND bile-soluble. Using both tests together confirms pneumococcus definitively. An optochin zone of 9–13mm is indeterminate — request bile solubility testing.

gpc_camp.mechanism: S. agalactiae produces CAMP factor (Christie–Atkins–Munch-Petersen protein), which binds to and modifies red blood cells, making them susceptible to complete lysis by S. aureus beta-lysin. The synergistic effect produces a characteristic arrowhead-shaped zone of enhanced haemolysis pointing toward the S. aureus streak.
gpc_camp.procedure: Streak test organism perpendicular to (but not touching) a central streak of S. aureus beta-lysin on blood agar. Incubate 35°C 24h. Arrowhead-shaped zone of enhanced (complete) haemolysis at the junction = positive.
gpc_camp.tip: Distinction tip: All Group B Streptococcus are CAMP-positive. S. agalactiae colonises the vagina in ~25% of pregnant women, and vertical transmission during birth causes neonatal meningitis and sepsis. Universal prenatal screening at 35–37 weeks is why this organism matters clinically.

gpr_spores.mechanism: Endospores are metabolically dormant, highly resistant structures formed by certain Gram-positive rods under nutrient stress. They appear as clear, refractile, unstained bodies inside or adjacent to rod-shaped cells on Gram stain. Spore-forming rods belong to only two clinically important genera: Bacillus (aerobic) and Clostridium (anaerobic).
gpr_spores.procedure: Examine Gram-stained slide under oil immersion (100×). Look for clear, oval or round unstained bodies within or adjacent to rod-shaped cells — these are endospores. The Schaeffer–Fulton spore stain (malachite green) can confirm if needed.
gpr_spores.tip: Distinction tip: If you see endospores, you have immediately narrowed to just two genera. The aerobe/anaerobe distinction then separates them completely. This is why spore observation is a powerful and efficient branch point.

gpr_oxygen.mechanism: Bacillus species are obligate or facultative aerobes and possess catalase and superoxide dismutase to manage reactive oxygen species. Clostridium species are obligate anaerobes — they lack these enzymes and oxygen is lethal (generates toxic superoxide radicals that they cannot neutralise).
gpr_oxygen.procedure: Observe growth conditions required or inoculate both aerobic and anaerobic environments. Most Bacillus grow well in ambient air; Clostridium requires anaerobic conditions (anaerobic jar with GasPak or anaerobic chamber).
gpr_oxygen.tip: Distinction tip: Clostridium toxins include some of the most potent biological toxins known. C. botulinum produces botulinum toxin (flaccid paralysis), C. tetani produces tetanospasmin (spastic paralysis), C. perfringens produces alpha-toxin (gas gangrene). Each mechanism is worth knowing.

gpr_catalase2.mechanism: Among non-sporing Gram-positive rods, catalase status is a key differentiator. Listeria and Corynebacterium are catalase-positive. Lactobacillus and Erysipelothrix are catalase-negative. This reflects their different oxygen-handling strategies.
gpr_catalase2.procedure: Add 3% H₂O₂ to colony on a glass slide. Bubbling = positive. Use CHOC or non-blood media to avoid false positives from blood agar plates.
gpr_catalase2.tip: Distinction tip: The two most clinically important non-sporing Gram-positive rods are Listeria (catalase-positive, tumbling motility) and Corynebacterium (catalase-positive, palisade arrangement, Chinese-letter appearance). Both are catalase-positive but have very distinct microscopic morphology.

gpr_motility.mechanism: Listeria monocytogenes is motile due to peritrichous flagella expressed at 20–25°C but not at 37°C (a critical detail). Its characteristic "tumbling" motility — end-over-end tumbling movement — is visible by wet mount or semi-solid agar stab. Corynebacterium is non-motile.
gpr_motility.procedure: Wet mount from liquid culture grown at 25°C. Examine under brightfield at 40×. Tumbling, end-over-end motility = Listeria. Alternatively, stab inoculate motility test agar at 25°C — umbrella-shaped growth pattern confirms motility.
gpr_motility.tip: Distinction tip: Listeria is tested at 25°C, not 37°C, because flagella are only expressed at room temperature. If you use a 37°C culture you will miss the motility and misidentify it. This is a classic exam trap question.

gn_fluor.mechanism: Pseudomonas fluorescens and P. aeruginosa produce pyoverdine (a yellow-green fluorescent siderophore/pigment) detectable under UV light at 365 nm. Agrobacterium does not produce this pigment despite also being oxidase-positive and mucoid. Fluorescence is a strong differentiator within oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods.
gn_fluor.procedure: Expose colonies on agar plate to UV light (365 nm Wood's lamp) in a darkened room. Yellow-green fluorescent glow under UV = Pseudomonas fluorescens/putida. Blue-green pigment visible in white light (pyocyanin) = P. aeruginosa. No fluorescence = not Pseudomonas.
gn_fluor.tip: Distinction tip: Note that this experiment did not include UV fluorescence testing — so if Pseudomonas was assigned, it was identified by elimination using oxidase, colony morphology, and RFLP. In a real lab, UV fluorescence would be a first-line test. Mentioning this limitation shows critical evaluation of the experimental design.

gn_mucoid.mechanism: Agrobacterium tumefaciens produces abundant extracellular polysaccharides (EPS), creating a distinctive slimy, mucoid colony morphology. This polysaccharide production is important for its biology as a plant pathogen — it facilitates attachment to plant cells. High EPS can also inhibit PCR by reducing DNA template availability.
gn_mucoid.procedure: Examine colony surface appearance macroscopically. Mucoid colonies: glistening, wet-looking surface, colonies tend to "string" when touched with a loop. Compare to other non-mucoid colonies on the same plate.
gn_mucoid.tip: Distinction tip: PCR failure in Agrobacterium is often due to transferring excess extracellular polysaccharide rather than cells — meaning low DNA template. If colony PCR fails for a mucoid colony, try diluting the colony suspension, re-picking with less material, or performing a brief DNA extraction first.

gn_motility2.mechanism: Differentiates motile Enterobacter from non-motile Klebsiella in citrate-positive isolates.
gn_motility2.procedure: Diffuse growth away from stab = motile. Growth confined to stab = non-motile.
gn_motility2.tip: Distinction tip: pair non-motility with slower urease positivity for Klebsiella confirmation.

gpc_hemolysis.mechanism: Haemolysis pattern is an early phenotypic split for Gram-positive cocci. Beta-haemolysis (complete clearing) suggests S. aureus, S. pyogenes, or S. agalactiae. Alpha-haemolysis (green partial lysis) suggests S. pneumoniae or viridans streptococci. Gamma haemolysis (no lysis) is common in Enterococcus and some CoNS.
gpc_hemolysis.procedure: Inspect blood agar after 18–24 h incubation. Clear halo = beta; green discolouration = alpha; no change = gamma. Use this alongside Gram stain and catalase rather than as a stand-alone test.
gpc_hemolysis.tip: Distinction tip: verbal examiners often ask what you observe before adding reagents. Naming haemolysis first shows systematic culture-plate interpretation.

gpc_coagulase_screen.mechanism: Slide coagulase detects bound coagulase (clumping factor). It is fast but less specific than tube coagulase because some coagulase-negative staphylococci (notably S. lugdunensis) can agglutinate and appear falsely positive.
gpc_coagulase_screen.procedure: Mix colony with saline and plasma on a slide. Immediate clumping is a positive screen. Always confirm positives with tube coagulase before reporting S. aureus.
gpc_coagulase_screen.tip: Distinction tip: never report S. aureus from slide coagulase alone; use tube coagulase confirmation to avoid S. lugdunensis misidentification.
gpc_coagulase_screen.yesLabel: Slide positive — confirm with tube test

gpc_bile.mechanism: S. pneumoniae autolyses in bile salts due to activation of its autolytic enzymes. Viridans streptococci remain intact. Bile solubility therefore confirms pneumococcus when optochin is susceptible or borderline.
gpc_bile.procedure: Add sodium deoxycholate (bile salts) to a dense suspension and incubate up to 30 min at 35–37°C. Clearing of turbidity = positive.
gpc_bile.tip: Distinction tip: use bile solubility when optochin zone is indeterminate (9–13 mm) to avoid overcalling pneumococcus.

gpr_h2s.mechanism: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae can produce H2S in TSI/KIA media, while Lactobacillus spp. are H2S-negative. This helps split catalase-negative, non-sporing Gram-positive rods.
gpr_h2s.procedure: Inoculate TSI/KIA with stab and streak. Blackening (especially in butt) indicates H2S production.
gpr_h2s.tip: Distinction tip: Erysipelothrix is associated with fish/animal exposure and can cause endocarditis — do not dismiss all catalase-negative rods as Lactobacillus.

gn_macconkey.mechanism: MacConkey agar gives an immediate screen of enteric Gram-negative rods. Lactose fermenters form pink/red colonies from acid production; non-lactose fermenters stay pale/colourless.
gn_macconkey.procedure: Review colony colour after incubation on MacConkey agar. Pink/red colonies = lactose fermenter. Colourless/pale colonies = non-lactose fermenter.
gn_macconkey.tip: Distinction tip: this is a frontline branch in routine labs and should be integrated before deeper biochemical testing.

gn_oxidase_lf.mechanism: Confirms whether a lactose fermenter is Enterobacteriaceae (oxidase-negative) or a less common oxidase-positive fermenter.
gn_oxidase_lf.procedure: Use oxidase reagent; purple-blue in 10–30 s is positive.
gn_oxidase_lf.tip: Distinction tip: classic coliforms (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) are oxidase-negative.

gn_indole_lf.mechanism: Indole positivity strongly suggests E. coli among common lactose fermenters.
gn_indole_lf.procedure: Tryptone broth + Kovacs reagent: red ring is positive.
gn_indole_lf.tip: Distinction tip: follow indole-negative isolates with citrate/VP and motility rather than stopping early.

gn_mug.mechanism: Most E. coli strains hydrolyse MUG to a fluorescent product, supporting rapid confirmation.
gn_mug.procedure: Inoculate MUG substrate and examine under 366 nm UV; fluorescence is positive.
gn_mug.tip: Distinction tip: ~95% of E. coli are MUG-positive; interpret with other tests for atypical strains.

gn_citrate.mechanism: Enterobacter and Klebsiella use citrate as sole carbon source (positive), while E. coli is typically citrate-negative.
gn_citrate.procedure: Inoculate Simmons citrate slant. Blue colour/growth = positive; green/no growth = negative.
gn_citrate.tip: Distinction tip: citrate and VP are the key IMViC gaps when indole alone is insufficient.

gn_urease_kleb.mechanism: Klebsiella is urease-positive, usually slower than Proteus. Urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia, alkalinising medium.
gn_urease_kleb.procedure: Urea broth/slant: pink shift within 24–48 h supports Klebsiella.
gn_urease_kleb.tip: Distinction tip: report timing — rapid urease suggests Proteus, slower positivity supports Klebsiella.

gn_oxidase_nlf.mechanism: Separates oxidase-negative enteric pathogens (Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus) from oxidase-positive non-fermenters or fastidious organisms.
gn_oxidase_nlf.tip: Distinction tip: oxidase-negative + non-lactose fermenter should trigger TSI/H2S workup.

gn_tsi.mechanism: TSI combines glucose/lactose/sucrose fermentation, gas, and H2S detection. H2S-positive blackening strongly supports Salmonella or Proteus among oxidase-negative non-lactose fermenters.
gn_tsi.procedure: Stab butt and streak slant; read at 18–24 h for K/A or A/A patterns, gas cracks, and black precipitate.
gn_tsi.tip: Distinction tip: in your notes, H2S-positive points to Salmonella; confirm Proteus by rapid urease/swarming.

gn_urease_rapid.mechanism: Proteus species are strongly and rapidly urease positive; Salmonella is urease negative.
gn_urease_rapid.procedure: Inoculate urea medium and observe early colour change. Rapid bright pink is positive.
gn_urease_rapid.tip: Distinction tip: rapid urease plus swarming motility is classic Proteus.

gn_shigella_motility.mechanism: Shigella is characteristically non-motile; many other enteric rods are motile.
gn_shigella_motility.procedure: Semi-solid motility medium: growth only along stab line is non-motile.
gn_shigella_motility.tip: Distinction tip: H2S-negative + non-motile strongly supports Shigella.

gn_choc.test: Growth requirement on CHOC agar / fastidious pattern
gn_choc.mechanism: Neisseria and Haemophilus are oxidase-positive but fastidious; they require enriched media and (for Haemophilus) X and V factors.
gn_choc.procedure: Assess growth on chocolate agar and factor dependence (X, V, XV disks) where available.
gn_choc.tip: Distinction tip: fastidious oxidase-positive isolates should not be forced into enteric decision branches.

gn_xv.mechanism: Haemophilus influenzae requires both X (hemin) and V (NAD) factors. Neisseria does not show this requirement pattern.
gn_xv.procedure: Use factor disk testing on supplemented agar: growth only around XV indicates Haemophilus.
gn_xv.tip: Distinction tip: this branch anchors the CHOC-agar section from your notes.

gn_betahem.mechanism: Aeromonas spp. are oxidase-positive water-associated rods that are frequently beta-haemolytic, unlike many other oxidase-positive rods in this branch.
gn_betahem.procedure: Inspect blood agar for clear haemolytic zones around colonies.
gn_betahem.tip: Distinction tip: oxidase-positive + beta-haemolysis should prompt Aeromonas consideration.

gpc_colony_colour.mechanism: Micrococcus species produce carotenoid pigments that create bright yellow colonies, while common coagulase-negative staphylococci are usually white or cream. Pigmentation therefore adds a practical phenotype split after coagulase negativity.
gpc_colony_colour.procedure: Inspect colony colour in good light after 18–24 h incubation. Bright yellow colonies suggest Micrococcus; white/cream colonies support CoNS and should proceed to novobiocin testing.
gpc_colony_colour.tip: Distinction tip: Micrococcus are catalase-positive cocci often arranged in tetrads and can be mistaken for staphylococci. Pair yellow pigment with tetrad morphology to justify the call confidently.

gn_smac.mechanism: Most E. coli ferment sorbitol and form pink colonies on SMAC. E. coli O157:H7 is typically sorbitol non-fermenting, producing colourless colonies. This is a critical public-health screen.
gn_smac.procedure: Inoculate SMAC and incubate overnight. Pink colonies indicate sorbitol fermentation; colourless colonies indicate sorbitol non-fermentation and require urgent confirmatory testing.
gn_smac.tip: Distinction tip: suspect STEC/O157 when sorbitol-negative E. coli is detected. Early lab escalation matters because antibiotic-induced lysis may increase Shiga toxin release and worsen HUS risk.

saureus.name: Staphylococcus aureus
saureus.clinical: Skin/soft tissue infections, nosocomial pneumonia, bacteraemia, endocarditis, toxic shock syndrome, food poisoning (heat-stable enterotoxin — not destroyed by cooking).
saureus.distinction: MRSA carries the mecA gene encoding PBP2a — a modified penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams, conferring resistance to all penicillins and cephalosporins. CHROMagar MRSA shows characteristic mauve colonies. This is a critical public health issue because MRSA infections cannot be treated with first-line beta-lactams.

sepidermidis.name: Staphylococcus epidermidis
sepidermidis.clinical: Nosocomial infections: prosthetic device infections (catheters, heart valves, joint replacements). Forms robust biofilm on plastic surfaces, protecting from antibiotics and host immune defences.
sepidermidis.distinction: Distinguishing true CoNS infection from skin contamination (the most common source of blood culture contamination) requires clinical judgement: multiple positive blood cultures from different sites, or a positive culture from an indwelling device, increase specificity. Biofilm formation is the pathogenic mechanism — the biofilm physically shields organisms from antibiotics.

ssaprophyticus.name: Staphylococcus saprophyticus
ssaprophyticus.clinical: UTIs in young, sexually active women — second most common cause after E. coli. Symptoms: dysuria, frequency, pyuria. Responds to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and nitrofurantoin.
ssaprophyticus.distinction: Novobiocin resistance is intrinsic, not acquired — it reflects a structural difference in the GyrB subunit of S. saprophyticus DNA gyrase. This is important because you cannot "de-resist" it with antibiotic stewardship — the resistance is biological, not epidemiological.

enterococcus.name: Enterococcus spp.
enterococcus.clinical: Normal GI flora that causes UTIs, wound infections, bacteraemia, and endocarditis in immunocompromised patients. E. faecalis and E. faecium are the most clinically important species.
enterococcus.distinction: VRE (vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus) has two main resistance mechanisms: VanA (acquired, high-level resistance to vancomycin AND teicoplanin) and VanB (lower-level, teicoplanin remains active). E. faecium is more often VRE than E. faecalis. Contact precautions and environmental decontamination are required — VRE can survive on surfaces for weeks.

spyogenes.name: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A)
spyogenes.clinical: Pharyngitis (strep throat), impetigo, scarlet fever, necrotising fasciitis, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Post-streptococcal sequelae: rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
spyogenes.distinction: Rheumatic fever results from molecular mimicry — anti-M protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac tissue (particularly the myosin heavy chain), causing autoimmune valve damage. This is why even uncomplicated strep throat warrants antibiotic treatment — not because the infection itself is dangerous, but to prevent the autoimmune complication.

spneumoniae.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
spneumoniae.clinical: Leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, bacterial meningitis, otitis media, and sinusitis. Responsible for significant morbidity globally.
spneumoniae.distinction: The polysaccharide capsule is the primary virulence factor — it inhibits opsonisation and prevents phagocytosis by blocking complement deposition. Asplenic patients are at extreme risk because the spleen is where encapsulated bacteria are cleared. PCV13 and PPSV23 vaccines target capsular polysaccharides (84+ serotypes exist).

sagalactiae.name: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B)
sagalactiae.clinical: Leading cause of neonatal meningitis and sepsis. Colonises vagina in ~25% of pregnant women. Universal prenatal screening at 35–37 weeks; intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin) if positive.
sagalactiae.distinction: CAMP factor is a pore-forming protein that binds to the altered red blood cell surface (modified by S. aureus beta-lysin) and completes lysis. The arrowhead points TOWARD the S. aureus streak — this directionality matters for interpretation. Intrapartum prophylaxis has reduced early-onset GBS disease by >80% in screened populations.

viridans.name: Viridans group Streptococci
viridans.clinical: Normal oral and GI flora. Causes subacute bacterial endocarditis (SBE) after dental procedures in patients with pre-existing valve abnormalities. S. mutans associated with dental caries.
viridans.distinction: SBE from viridans streptococci results from transient bacteraemia during dental work seeding damaged or prosthetic valves. The organisms are not inherently virulent — it is the damaged valve surface that provides a substrate for colonisation. Antibiotic prophylaxis before high-risk dental procedures is recommended only for specific high-risk cardiac conditions (prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis).

bacillus.name: Bacillus spp.
bacillus.clinical: B. anthracis: anthrax (cutaneous, pulmonary, gastrointestinal — spores used in bioterrorism). B. cereus: food poisoning (two types: emetic from fried rice, diarrhoeal from meat/vegetables). B. subtilis/licheniformis: occasional opportunistic infections.
bacillus.distinction: B. anthracis is non-motile (distinguishes it from other Bacillus which are usually motile) and lacks haemolysis. Spores are the infective form — extraordinarily resistant to heat, desiccation, and chemicals. The toxin complex (protective antigen + lethal factor + oedema factor) is the primary virulence mechanism.

clostridium.name: Clostridium spp.
clostridium.clinical: C. difficile: antibiotic-associated colitis; C. tetani: tetanus (spastic paralysis); C. botulinum: botulism (flaccid paralysis, food/wound/infant); C. perfringens: gas gangrene, food poisoning.
clostridium.distinction: C. tetani produces tetanospasmin (blocks inhibitory interneurones → spastic paralysis — "lock jaw"). C. botulinum produces botulinum toxin (blocks ACh release at NMJ → flaccid paralysis). Opposite clinical presentations from related organisms — this distinction is a frequent exam question because the mechanism determines the presentation.

listeria.name: Listeria monocytogenes
listeria.clinical: Meningitis/encephalitis in neonates, elderly, and immunocompromised. Pregnancy: crosses placenta causing fetal abortion or neonatal infection. Foodborne outbreaks: deli meats, soft cheeses, raw milk.
listeria.distinction: Listeria can replicate at 4°C — refrigeration does NOT eliminate it. It is an intracellular pathogen that uses actin-based motility (ActA protein polymerises host actin into "comet tails") to spread directly between cells without exposing itself to extracellular antibiotics or antibodies. This explains why immunosuppression is such a strong risk factor.

coryne.name: Corynebacterium spp.
coryne.clinical: C. diphtheriae: diphtheria (pseudomembrane in throat, diphtheria toxin causes myocarditis, neuritis, adrenal necrosis). C. jeikeium and C. urealyticum: opportunistic nosocomial infections in immunocompromised.
coryne.distinction: Diphtheria toxin (encoded by bacteriophage β) inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylating elongation factor EF-2. The pseudomembrane in the pharynx is grey-white and bleeds when removed — this distinguishes it from viral pharyngitis. Low population immunity (declining vaccination rates) makes this organism a recurring public health concern.

lactobacillus.name: Lactobacillus spp.
lactobacillus.clinical: Generally non-pathogenic normal flora of GI tract and vagina. Maintain vaginal pH through lactic acid production. Rare infections in immunocompromised patients. Used as probiotics.
lactobacillus.distinction: The vancomycin resistance of Lactobacillus is intrinsic (not acquired) — its cell wall precursors terminate in D-Lac rather than D-Ala, giving low vancomycin affinity. This is biologically significant: it means PCR-based VRE testing can give false positives if Lactobacillus DNA contaminates a clinical specimen.

pseudomonas.name: Pseudomonas fluorescens / aeruginosa

path.t: Growth requirement on CHOC agar / fastidious pattern

pseudomonas.clinical: P. aeruginosa: major opportunistic pathogen — ventilator-associated pneumonia, burn wound infections, CF lung colonisation, UTIs, keratitis. Intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics.
pseudomonas.distinction: P. aeruginosa has exceptional intrinsic antibiotic resistance: constitutive AmpC beta-lactamase, efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM etc.), and low outer membrane permeability. Treatment requires anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, meropenem) — standard penicillin is completely ineffective. In the module's RFLP analysis, APA1 digestion shows a unique pattern for Pseudomonas that distinguishes it from E. coli.

agrobacterium.name: Agrobacterium tumefaciens

path.t: Growth requirement on CHOC agar / fastidious pattern

agrobacterium.clinical: Plant pathogen — causes crown gall disease by transferring T-DNA into plant cells via a Ti plasmid. Limited human pathogenicity (rare opportunistic infections in immunocompromised). Widely used in plant genetic engineering as a DNA delivery vehicle.
agrobacterium.distinction: Colony PCR failure in mucoid organisms is often caused by excess extracellular polysaccharide competing with DNA template. A 1:10 dilution of the picked colony suspension or a brief alkaline lysis step improves template availability and PCR success.

ecoli.name: Escherichia coli
features: TSI: A/A (acid slant/acid butt), gas, no H2S
ecoli.clinical: Most common cause of UTIs, neonatal meningitis (K1 capsule strains), traveller's diarrhoea. Pathogenic variants: ETEC, EHEC (O157:H7 — HUS risk), EPEC, EIEC, EAEC.
ecoli.distinction: E. coli O157:H7 produces Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin) which inhibits protein synthesis in endothelial cells, causing haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + renal failure. Antibiotic treatment is CONTRAINDICATED in EHEC because lysis releases more toxin. This is a critical clinical distinction.

klebsiella.name: Klebsiella pneumoniae
klebsiella.clinical: Community-acquired pneumonia (especially in alcoholics, diabetics — "currant jelly" sputum from haemorrhagic necrosis). Hospital-acquired UTIs, bacteraemia. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) and carbapenemase (KPC) strains are critical healthcare threats.
klebsiella.distinction: Klebsiella's large polysaccharide capsule produces mucoid colonies (similar appearance to Agrobacterium but Gram-negative). The capsule is antiphagocytic. Hypervirulent Klebsiella (hvKP) strains produce "hypermucoviscous" colonies that form a string >5mm when touched with a loop — the "string test" is a quick bedside screen for hvKP, which has higher mortality than classical KPC strains.

other_oxpos.name: Other oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod

path.t: Growth requirement on CHOC agar / fastidious pattern

other_oxpos.clinical: Further testing required: Aeromonas, Plesiomonas, Vibrio, Chromobacterium, Alcaligenes, or other oxidase-positive non-fermenters. Additional tests: glucose fermentation, motility, growth on TCBS agar.
other_oxpos.distinction: When you reach an ambiguous result in the decision tree, the distinction-level response is to say: "Further biochemical characterisation would be required, specifically X and Y tests, to differentiate between [list of candidates]." Demonstrating that you know what additional tests to use is as important as knowing when to use them.

enterobacter.name: Enterobacter spp.
enterobacter.clinical: Nosocomial opportunist causing pneumonia, UTIs, line infections, and bacteraemia, especially in ICU settings.
enterobacter.distinction: Enterobacter cloacae complex can derepress AmpC beta-lactamase during therapy, causing treatment failure with 3rd-generation cephalosporins.

salmonella.name: Salmonella spp.
salmonella.clinical: Causes enterocolitis and, for typhoidal serovars, systemic typhoid/paratyphoid fever.
salmonella.distinction: H2S production is a key practical differentiator from Shigella in routine Enterobacteriaceae workups.

shigella.name: Shigella spp.
features: TSI: K/A, no gas, H2S negative
shigella.clinical: Causes bacillary dysentery with fever, abdominal cramps, and bloody diarrhoea.
shigella.distinction: Because infectious dose is low, person-to-person spread is efficient; strict hygiene and outbreak control are essential.

proteus.name: Proteus spp.
features: TSI: K/A with H2S positive (black precipitate)
proteus.clinical: Common cause of complicated UTIs and catheter-associated infection. Urease releases ammonia, alkalinising urine and promoting magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) kidney stone formation.
proteus.distinction: Urease-driven alkalinisation promotes magnesium ammonium phosphate stone formation and persistent catheter-associated infection.

aeromonas.name: Aeromonas spp.
aeromonas.clinical: Associated with wound infections after freshwater exposure and gastroenteritis.
aeromonas.distinction: Clinical context (freshwater trauma, leech therapy, aquatic exposure) is often decisive when Aeromonas is suspected.

haemophilus.name: Haemophilus influenzae

path.t: Growth requirement on CHOC agar / fastidious pattern

haemophilus.clinical: Causes otitis, sinusitis, COPD exacerbations, and invasive disease (especially unvaccinated populations).
haemophilus.distinction: Factor dependence testing (XV requirement) is the classic bench method to distinguish Haemophilus from Neisseria.

neisseria.name: Neisseria spp.

path.t: Growth requirement on CHOC agar / fastidious pattern

neisseria.clinical: Includes N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae, causing meningitis/septicaemia and gonorrhoea respectively.
neisseria.distinction: Always correlate organism-level ID with site and morphology because commensal Neisseria can colonise mucosal sites.

other_lf.name: Other lactose-fermenting coliform
other_lf.clinical: Could include Citrobacter, Serratia, or atypical Enterobacteriaceae depending on full panel.
other_lf.distinction: Use expanded IMViC and MALDI-TOF when key confirmatory tests are discordant.

other_nlf.name: Other non-lactose fermenting enteric rod
features: Profile does not fully match Salmonella/Shigella/Proteus
other_nlf.clinical: May represent Morganella, Providencia, Yersinia, or uncommon enteric pathogens.
other_nlf.distinction: If motility and TSI are discordant, escalate to comprehensive biochemical or molecular identification.

erysipelothrix.name: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae
erysipelothrix.clinical: Causes erysipeloid skin infection in fish handlers, butchers, and veterinarians; can rarely cause endocarditis.
erysipelothrix.distinction: Occupational history is critical: handling fish, shellfish, or animals strongly raises suspicion for Erysipelothrix.

micrococcus.name: Micrococcus luteus
micrococcus.clinical: Usually low virulence and often a contaminant, but can cause opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients or those with indwelling devices.
micrococcus.distinction: Micrococcus can be separated from staphylococci by tetrad arrangement and pigment production. In practical exams, explicitly saying "yellow pigmented catalase-positive cocci in tetrads" demonstrates high-quality bench interpretation.

ecoli_o157.name: Escherichia coli O157:H7 (STEC)
features: TSI: A/A, gas, usually no H2S
ecoli_o157.clinical: Causes haemorrhagic colitis and can progress to haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), especially in children and older adults.
ecoli_o157.distinction: In suspected STEC, avoid empiric antibiotics until specialist guidance because bacterial lysis can increase Shiga toxin release and worsen HUS risk. Prioritise toxin testing and public-health notification.
